utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant, Mr. Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present. We have a witness scheduled for today. We can call the witness into the courtroom now. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Could you stand up, please. And tell me whether you can hear what I'm saying interpreted into your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. First of all, you should tell me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ivo Mrso. I'm the son of Mirko and Jela. I was born in 1938 in Bugojno. I live in Bugojno now and work in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were born in 1938. Do you know the exact date or only the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 20th of March. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I graduated as an agricultural engineer. I now work in the forestry and water department as an assistant to the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been called here to testify with regard to certain facts. But before you do so, you must make a solemn declaration. The usher, who is by your side, will show you a text. Could you read it out in your own language, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Prosecution takes the floor and asks you some questions, I have to inform you about the testimony you will be giving here. As you have made a solemn declaration, it is your duty to tell the truth. If you give false testimony, you could be prosecuted for having given false testimony and there could be a sentence, a term of imprisonment as punishment. In the course of the questions put to you, if anything you say when answering questions could at a subsequent time be used against you in any prosecution, you ought to know that according to the Rules of the Tribunal, in such a case, given that you have testified at the request of the Prosecution, whatever you say can't be used to prosecute you. In addition, when questions are put to you, try to answer the questions as fully as possible. Try to provide precise answers. And if you don't understand a question, ask the person putting the question to you to ask you to question again -- ask you the question again in order to ensure that your answer is clear. If you don't know the answer to a question, tell us. Or if you have forgotten, tell us that you can no longer remember. Representatives of the Prosecution, who are to your right, will be asking you questions in a minute. After they have concluded their examination-in-chief, the Defence, who are to your left, will also ask you a series of questions. They will proceed with their cross-examination. The three Judges, who are before you, can also ask you questions at any time if they feel that it is necessary, in order to clarify responses to either of the parties. If there are any difficulties that you feel you face in the course of your testimony, please inform us of this fact. Having provided you with this information, the Prosecution may now proceed with its examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mrso. Mr. Mrso, can you please inform --

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber whether today it's the first time that you are testifying before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to when earlier on you have testified before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I think it was on the 10th of July, 2000, in the Dario Kordic case. I was a witness for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what were the main areas, the main issues you covered in the course of this testimony in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, there were situations in Central Bosnia that were concerned, and the issue of Bugojno and the connections that Mr. Kordic had with Bugojno, in the military and political sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, are you or have you been married?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. I was married. I'm divorced now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about the ethnicity of your divorced, ex-wife.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: She was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to when you were divorced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, you already informed the Trial Chamber that you were born in Bugojno. Can you please also tell us where you grew up.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where did you live from 1990 onwards?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you ever joined the JNA, Mr. Mrso?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. I did my military service, from 1965 to 1966. It lasted for one year, in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Mrso, whilst you were living in Bugojno that you joined the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform us as to when you joined the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, I started talking to them in 1990. I established contact with them in 1990. But I think I joined officially in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please tell us for what the acronym HDZ stands for.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It's the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After you joined the HDZ in 1991, officially in 1991, did there come a time that you were elected to the municipal committee in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, not that year. In 1992, I was in a local branch, Vrbas II, and as such I later became a member of the town committee of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please tell us for how long you have been a member of the town committee of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Until the 18th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Mrso, when you were elected president of the municipal council in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform us as to when and for how long, if so.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Those were the first elections after the war, from 1996 to the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the ethnicities living in Bugojno in 1990.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: There were Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, and others. About 35 per cent were Croats; 42 per cent were Muslims; and 18 per cent were Serbs; and then there were the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What do these percentages mean in numbers of inhabitants, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: There were about 16.100 Croats, about 2.000 more Muslims, and about 8.000 Serbs, and the others, I think -- if I remember this correctly, I think there were about 5.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, about "2.000 more Muslims" means that there were about 18.000 Muslims living in Bugojno at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether there has been a change in the number of Croats living in Bugojno after 1990.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Not after 1990, immediately after 1990. In 1993, when the attack was carried out, then about 3.000 Croats remained. Because of various forms of maltreatment, by the end of 1993 there were only about 900 of us who had remained, because people were fleeing, leaving the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, for clarification, Mr. Mrso, there were about 16.100 Croats living in Bugojno prior to the war, and this number diminished within the year 1993 to about 900?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: At the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, how would you describe the relationship between the Muslims and the Croats in Bugojno in late 1992 and in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, in my assessment, as an inhabitant, they were on good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did there come a time when this good relationship changed?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And as to when was it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, in the second half of 1992. It had already started deteriorating then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the reasons why the relationships deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, as far as I know, I think that the idea of defence and policies -- well, the Croats thought that they had to defend themselves from the Serbs, because the Serbs had already attacked Donji Vakuf and they were moving out the Muslims. I think that that idea, the idea of defence, at least in Bugojno, caused differences of opinion as to who would have control. And then there were statements given by Muslim leaders. There were Alija's statements about the attack on the Ravno and the fact that that wasn't their war, although there were Croats there, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Alija's statement, whom are you referring to when you say "Alija"?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time when this deteriorating relationship between the Croats and the Muslims caused an open outbreak of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. In my opinion, there were negotiations in order to establish a joint Territorial Defence. And then according to the statements that were given -- I wasn't part of the military and political structure, I was a party member -- But there were obstructions, there were fights as to who would be in charge, what sort of leadership there would be. And I don't think that this really ever came to life in Bugojno. I don't think it ever assumed real shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And when did it come to an open outbreak of hostilities between the Croats and the Muslims in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, as I said, towards the end of 1992 there were provocations. And then in 1993, the same thing happened. And as there was no power structure established in Bugojno on the basis of the electoral results, the Muslims weren't in agreement, although the HDZ party had won the elections at the time. At the end of 1992, the party members from the SDA were going their own ways. There were no longer agreements for common defence. So around October and November I suggested to Mr. Matko Lucic, as the HDZ president, and the deputy president, Mirko Antunovic. I said we should go and see Dzevad Mlaco, who was the SDA president. At the time, they had already moved to the municipality building in Bugojno, to the lower floors of that building. So we went to see him. I saw that there were some bags of sand that had been set in front for protection. And I insisted on saying openly that there were provocations between the Muslims and Croats and that this was not all right. I said that the people should be openly told that this had no sense. We had -- we spoke about this over coffee, us people of Bugojno. And the gentleman listened to this in a very casual way. He had a smile on his face. And I could see that he wasn't taking this very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, you already mentioned Mr. Dzevad Mlaco, as the former head of the SDA in Bugojno. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the key players on the Muslim side in both on the civilian side and on the military side.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, Dzevad Mlaco was part of the civilian structures. He was the SDA president. And later, after they had established a Crisis Staff -- or rather, a War Presidency -- he was the president of the War Presidency. I later found out that in that War Presidency there were nine to 11 members. Among them was Mr. Abdulah Jelec and then Kemal Dzafic - I remember that name. Ismet Hadzibegovic, also known as Dursum, Zejir Mlivo, as the deputy president of the War Presidency, and there were some others too. Redzep Dolovac. I later found out he was in charge of logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who was in charge, Mr. Mrso, of the Muslim forces in Bugojno in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I can't tell you about that for the entire year 1993. But after the attack, after I had left the camp, they told me who the person in charge was. It was Enes Handzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Selmo Cikotic, and if so, do you know his position in 1993 in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. Selmo Cikotic was the military commander of the unit for Bugojno. He was the main one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mrso, do you know a name called Dautovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Senad Dautovic, yes. He was also the president of the War Presidency. He was the chief of police. And I don't know whether he performed any other military duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The police you are referring, to was it the civilian or the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They were mostly military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And was Mr. Dautovic commander of the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. When I spoke to Dzevad Mlaco, who sent me to Dautovic, he told me he was in charge of the camp on behalf of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And which camp, Mr. Mrso, are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't understand. When you say "camp," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You said, at least according to the transcript, that you have been told that Mr. Dautovic was in charge of the camp on behalf of the police. And my question is: Which camp are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Iskra Stadium camp. I apologise. The first translation I got was the literal translation "camp," and that was not the word that I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Mrso. Mr. Mrso, did there come a time prior to the outbreak of the conflicts in Bugojno, did there come a time when you noticed foreigners arriving in the area of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. As early as 1992, you could notice them. There were fewer of them at the beginning, but their number increased in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To one of the questions by my learned friend, the witness replied that Senad Dautovic - that's line 14, page 10 - I don't know what he said, but it says here in the transcript that he was also the president of the War Presidency. And the witness didn't say that. The witness said that the president of the War Presidency told him that Senad Dautovic was in charge of the military police. That's how I understood his words. So can we please have it clarified with the witness. Line 14: "Yes, Senad Dautovic. Yes. He was also the president of the War Presidency." The witness never said that Senad Dautovic was the president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Defence for this observation. This observation understood the witness in the language that the witness speaks. It seems that we have a problem with the interpretation. Let's resolve this issue. Can the Prosecution please rephrase that question in order to clarify the reply. The question concerns Mr. Senad Dautovic and his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso -- thank you very much, Mr. President. Mr. Mrso, you understood the discussion in respect to Mr. Senad Dautovic. Was he also the president of the War Presidency in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. He was just one of the members. Dzevad Mlaco was its president throughout all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Mrso, for this clarification. We were about to talk about foreigners arriving in Bugojno prior to the open outbreak of the conflict. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to when you for the first time noticed these foreigners arriving in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: As early as 1992, we could notice them, especially when there were rallies on market days, on Fridays, when the market was -- open market was held in Bugojno. They stood out by their different clothes. I didn't pay too much attention to them to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Even if you didn't pay too much attention to them, can you inform the Trial Chamber from which countries they came from, as far as you can tell.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that. I never spoke to any of these people. I didn't ask them anything. I just noticed them as I was passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how can you tell, Mr. Mrso, that these individuals were foreigners? What was the difference in comparison to the Bugojno locals?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Their clothes were different. Their skin colour was different. Most of them had beards. Some of them had turbans. Some of them wore headpieces on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What sort of turbans are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: That's a headpiece for the head, and it's in the shape of a turban. I can't give you any other word for that. Some had bandannas. Some had turbans. Some had nothing on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Mrso, when you were arrested in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please tell us when.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: 24 July, around 10.00. Between 10.00 and 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please provide the Trial Chamber with some details about this arrest.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: On the 18th of July, when the attack was carried out, I was in the town. And I found it strange that the town was empty. I was looking to buy some newspapers. Then I returned home. I had obtained a newspaper from a friend. I was home alone. I was reading the newspaper. And then between 5.00 and 6.00 I noticed there were people moving in a haste in the streets. From my window, I could notice people in military uniforms running to and fro. I didn't know what was going on. I didn't go out. I didn't leave my house. I remained sitting in my house reading the newspaper. Sometime between 11.00 and 12.00, I went to bed. And then around 4.00 I woke up. Somebody was banging at my door and shouting, "Open up." I was afraid. I asked, "Who is it? Who should I open the door for?" After a silence, somebody opened fire from the outside and all the glass on the windows and the doors shattered. I threw myself on the floor, and I waited to see what would happen. After that, there was a period of silence. Nobody said anything. I got dressed very slowly, and that's how I was, until the dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards, Mr. Mrso?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In the morning, when it was already daylight, I saw what had happened. I didn't know what to do. I just collected the pieces of glass. I opened my door, unlocked my door. I also collected the glass from the ground in front of the door, and I went to the garbage bin. As I was coming home, there were three shots at me. One bullet hit the door. I ran into my house. I closed the door behind me. And from then onwards, I didn't dare step out of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And after all these events you were just detailing, Mr. Mrso, have you actually been arrested and brought to somewhere?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, not on that day. Around 11.00, again somebody knocked on my door and introduced himself as Reuf. Reuf is an acquaintance of mine, a friend of mine. I opened the door, and there we were standing at my doorstep. He asked me whether I was alive. Again, somebody opened fire at us. I drew him into my house. We were both scared. And then he said, "What now?" And I said, "Nothing. You'd better go, because if you had been killed just a little while ago, I would have been blamed for that." He didn't want to leave, but I insisted. And then he went. He used to live next door, and that's where he went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And after Reuf, Mr. Reuf went to his house next door, what did happen to you afterwards?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I was in the house. I didn't know what to do. Sometime around 4.00 he came again. He hid. I opened a window for him this time, and he entered through the window. We talked, and then he told me that the Muslims had launched an attack, that all the Croat houses had been ransacked, that some Croats had been arrested, that some were being taken away, that the collections centre had been set up in the neighbourhood. And he told me, "You should either flee or come to my place." I didn't know what to do. I was puzzled. And then I said, "If they're ransacking all the houses, they'll find me at your place and you will be in trouble." He insisted we jump through the window, and we crawled all the way to his house, where I hid in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did there come a time, Mr. Mrso, when you were found hiding in the basement of Mr. Reuf's house?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. On the following day, on Tuesday around 10.00, we heard some noise in my courtyard. We heard shots. We had an explosion, one or two explosions. There were some noise, some shouting. I didn't dare come out. He did, however. They shouted, "Open the door, Ustasha. We are going to kill you." And finally, when there was no answer from the door, they broke into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And after they broke into the house, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: We stayed in his basement. And on the following day, he went on a reconnoitring mission and then he noticed that another neighbour, another Muslim neighbour, had taken my key, and I was angry. I intervened with another person and told him to deliver them a message to this Fuko to return my key. Otherwise I won't be too happy. And then half an hour later my key was returned. Then I went to my house. Everything had been ransacked. A lot of things had been taken away. Almost everything had been taken away. The only things that remained were bigger pieces of furniture. I tidied up a little together with him and decided to stay on in the house no matter what.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These were the days from the 18th of the 22nd of July, Mr. Mrso. What happened to you on the 24th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: When I decided to go back home and stay there, a little while later two people came. One of them was a neighbour of mine, and another one was a teacher, another Muslim, and a third person was with them. They told me that they would ransack my house again. I said, "Why should you do that? You've already done it. You've taken whatever there was to be taken away." And I asked them, "What are you looking for?" They said, "Arms." I said, "Well, okay. Be my guest." They didn't find anything. They told me to stay put, to be at home. And no sooner did they leave, some other people came. One of them I knew. He was the son of an acquaintance of mine. I said, "What now?" And they said, "Somebody was shooting from this house." I said, "How could anybody shoot? I wasn't home. There's nobody home. And where were the shots directed?" "They were directed towards the stadium." I said, "Well, this is impossible, because my house is lower." And I said, "How come you think that somebody was shooting from the house? The house had been ransacked. There was nobody in the house. There's nothing in the house, no arms. Nobody was shooting from the house."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, may I please stop you there. The 24th of July, 1993. Have you been arrested on the 24th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, I have to say that the two men who had ransacked my house came again. They told me that I should leave the house and leave the door unlocked. I asked them where they were taking me. They said they were taking me to a Croat house nearby where all the other Croats had already been gathered. I said, "I don't want to do that. I want to stay in my house." They insisted. They almost forced me to go. I had to leave my house open and I had to go to that other Croat house. The owner of that house was Adolf Tomas, a neighbour of mine. I found the other Croats from my street there, and there were also three or four guards whom I also knew. They were also my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And whilst you were staying in your neighbour Tomas's house, did there come a time when you have been arrested on the 24th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I spent the night there. And I was planning on escaping from there. When I told them that I wanted to escape, they were afraid and they told me, "What if they catch you? Something bad might happen to us." So I changed my mind. I stayed on. We were looking through the window, and we could see our houses being looted, some of our houses already being moved in by Muslim families that had been expelled from Donji Vakuf. On the following morning, around 10.00 I hear a voice shouting, "Is Ivo Mrso here?" And the owner says, "Yes, he is." And I went out. There were some people there. I asked them, "Where are you taking me?" And they said, "What do you care? You don't need to know." There were three soldiers with armbands on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mrso, was there anything written on their armbands?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Those were armbands of different colours, red, green, and so on. And on some of them the inscription was "MOS."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, what does "MOS" stand for?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time. I asked some of my acquaintances, and they told me that the "MOS" stands for Muslim Liberation Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After you were arrested by members of the MOS, where have you been brought to?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They took me and two other Croats - Josip Rupnik and I can't remember the name of the second person - to a street that we call Kraj Donji [as interpreted]. As we arrived there, there were some soldiers sitting on the fence of one house, and they were shouting towards us, "Why are you taking these Ustashas with you? Why don't you kill them?" They put us in a garage. Somebody kicked me from behind, so I actually fell into the garage. In the garage, I already found some people. The garage was full of people. People were scared. And later on I recognised some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How many people, Mr. Mrso, did you find in the garage?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Later on, when I calmed down a little, I realised there were about 30 people or so, if not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic background of these 30 people or so, if not more?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the Croats in this garage, were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They were both, civilians and soldiers. They didn't allow us to talk. They told us to bow our heads, to put our heads between our knees, and that we should not talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who are the people that didn't allow you to talk? Were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And soldiers of what military organisation?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume that they were members of this MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, you informed the Trial Chamber that you were subjected to mistreatments once you arrived at the garage. Were there other detainees who were mistreated in the garage?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: When I was put in that garage, when that person kicked me and pushed me into the garage, one soldier with a bandanna around his forehead was waving a sabre, and he was cursing us. He was calling us names. He was shouting that we should all be killed, and so on and so forth. And as I was sitting closest to him, when he turned around I recognised him. I knew him from before. And then he said, "What are you doing here?" I said, "I don't know. I did not come of my own will." And then he said, "Let this man go through the far end of the garage and don't you touch him, any of you."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Mrso, any other prisoners being subjected to mistreatment in the garage?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: As I sat down, or -- I don't know how else to put it -- in that garage I had to bow my head but I could still peek and I could still see that there was a man lying on the floor half naked. His hands were tied behind his back. And another person was sitting on a chair, and his legs were in a water bucket. And the guards kept on shouting at him to press his legs further. They were hitting him and beating him. I asked a neighbour of mine, "Zoran, why are they doing that?" And Zoran told me, "This is some kind of torture. It is terrible, because it causes cramps in one's legs." And you could actually tell by looking at the person's face that he was suffering terribly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the guards who were hitting and beating this prisoner, were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. They were all in military uniforms, and they were all armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were they Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Mrso, when you were transferred from the garage to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: We spent one night in that garage. It was a night of terror. We were not given any food. We didn't have any water. It was cramped. It was dirty. They took people from the garage. They would beat them in front of the garage. Their shouts were terrible. And it all lasted up to 5.00 in the morning. Then they ordered us to get into a truck. We had to get into the truck single-file with our hands behind our heads. And one person that I also knew was shouting, "Ustasha, you should not be getting onto this truck. You should all be killed on the spot."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where did the truck bring you to?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: We didn't know as we were being driven. When the truck pulled over, I realised that we had been brought in front of the nunnery, which they called Marxist Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this building, the Marxist Centre, also known as the old convent in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, that's what Croats used to call it and still call it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And once you arrived at the old convent in Bugojno, what did happen to you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They put us in one of the larger rooms on the first floor. We found some people there whom I also knew. They were all inhabitants of the neighbourhood of Gaj. They told us that they had been arrested, taken to Karadza [phoen] in a shed, and then that they were brought to the convent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The time you've been detained at the old convent in Bugojno, did you spend the whole time on the first floor of this building?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. For one period of time, no one came to see us or tell us anything. We stayed in that room. And two hours later they came and said, "Let's go." And then we went in single file. We took the flight of stairs to the basement. There was a little table there. One man was sitting down. There were two who were standing. I know Mr. Safet Krslak. We were told to take our belts off and our laces out of our shoes and everything out of our pockets and put it on the table and we were told to go to the basement then. And I refused to do that. I didn't want to take my belt off. I said my trousers would fall down. I didn't want to take the laces out of my shoes, and so on. And as I knew this person called Krslak, I even said, "What's wrong with you? What do you want?" And then I went down into the basement like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the basement of the old convent building in Bugojno, were there also other detainees?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, it was empty. I was one of the first to enter the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time when other people were forced to join you in the basement of the old convent?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. When night had fallen, there was a piece of paper that I found. I had a piece -- I had a pencil on me, and I wrote down the names of the people who were there. I wrote down the names of 73 persons; naturally excluding the ones who had remained upstairs, who were from Gaj. They didn't go down into the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And these 73 persons in the basement of the old convent, what was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And these 73 Croats, were they civilians and/or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They were both civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were younger detainees imprisoned in the basement of the old convent in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. There were minors there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how old were they?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: One of them was 15 years old; another one 16; and I think there was someone who was 14 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the sanitary conditions in the basement of the old convent building in Bugojno whilst you were detained there.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, well, they were non-existent. The basement was fairly dirty. Later on they gave us some sort of bucket and shut the door and we had nothing else apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber for how many days you had to stay in the basement of the old convent building.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Sunday, Monday. I think on Tuesday I was moved back to the floor; maybe it was Wednesday. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, I'm now going to show you a photograph, and the photograph will appear on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Chamber and Defence counsel, we have the nine hard copies available for distribution.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: This is the convent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Please wait a second, Mr. Mrso. I will ask you some questions in relation to this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the meantime, for the information of the Chamber and Defence counsel, this photograph has been taken in 2002 in the course of the investigation against the accused Hadzihasanovic and Kubura. Can one of the hard copies please be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you can see on the photograph in front of you.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I can see a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please tell us which building you are seeing.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, the usual term that we use is a convent. It's a nunnery. I went to primary school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And is this the convent building you were detained?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please date and sign this photograph.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It's the 9th today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Completely correct. Today is the 9th of February.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution intends to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be P56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, I'm now going to show you another photograph. Again, it will appear on the screen in front of you, and you will be provided with a hard copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the information of the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel, this photograph has been taken also in 2002, in the course of the investigation against the accused Hadzihasanovic and Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please tell us what you can see on this photograph in front of you.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, this appears to be the basement in the convent. I can recognise it because of the bricks which form the floor of the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the basement of the old convent building you were detained together with 33 detainees in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Not 33; 73. But yes, that's the basement in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Mrso. Can you please again date and sign this photograph.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution intends to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, whilst you were detained together with the other 73 prisoners in the basement of the old convent building you just identified, did you become aware of any beatings?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber about these beatings.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, they took Mario Glisic out, for example. That very evening on a Sunday three men turned up and they said, "Come on, Mario Glisic." They took him out and they hadn't even shut the door. They started beating him. And you could hear his groaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other detainee who was beaten?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Vlatko Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. That's the person I found in the garage. He was half naked and lying down. Later I saw him in that basement. I asked him whether he was cold and whether he wanted my windproof jacket. He's the son of a school friend of mine. I went to primary school with his father. He said that it wasn't necessary, that he had received some sort of a shirt. He said that if necessary, if he felt cold, he would ask me for this jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Mrso, whether this Vlatko Kapetanovic was also beaten whilst you were in the old convent building?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: While I was in the basement, he wasn't, because the following day in the morning they took him away immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who was guarding the prisoners in the old convent building in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, there were soldiers who could be seen there all the time. If they came down, they would open the door. You could see them. They were soldiers. As to what happened outside the building, I don't know. As to what happened in the building further up and outside, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the soldiers who guarded the old convent building and guarded the prisoners, were these the people who took Mario Glisic out for a beating?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what military formation did these soldiers form part of?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I really don't know. I didn't dare ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you seen these soldiers wearing any insignia?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, at the time they still wore those headbands of various colours, and some of them had the inscription "MOS" on them; some didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the old convent building in Bugojno, have you been visited by somebody?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: That evening - I think it was already dark - Enes Handzic came. They opened a door for him. And from the door he said that we shouldn't be afraid, that everything would be all right. He had brought some tobacco with him -- not cigarettes, but tobacco. And he was there for two or three minutes and then left. The door was closed, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Enes Handzic, did he actually visit the basement of the old convent building in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. But what he said was from the door, which was open, the door to the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once Mr. Handzic visited the basement of the old convent building in Bugojno, was he able to see the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: We were all at the door and waiting to see what he would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the position of Enes Handzic at the time.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't know what position he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you get to know afterwards what position he held at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When I got out of the camp, I found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what did you find out, Mr. Mrso?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, when I got out, I immediately started establishing contacts with gentlemen in positions of power, with Dzevad Mlaco, as president of the War Presidency. I went to see him because people told me that various things were happening in the camp, et cetera. So we agreed to establish contact and when I told him about what was going on in the camp, he said this was the responsibility of Mr. Enes Handzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And have you been informed whilst talking to these people about the position of Enes Handzic? What was his role at the time, if any?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I remember -- according to what I remember, he was the chief of security. What kind of security, what sort of formation, I don't know. What is important for me is to know the first and last name of this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was in charge of the civilian or the military security?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I think he was in charge of military security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you been visited -- have you and the other detainees, Mr. Mrso, being visited by somebody else whilst you were detained at the old convent building in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. When I moved out of the basement, I asked someone who was in the building, who worked there as a receptionist or something like that -- perhaps he was a guard too. He was from Donji Vakuf. I knew him. And when we asked to go to the toilet or to have water to drink or to wash ourselves with, I said, "Please tell them to move me up. It's terrible down here. Tell them about this." I said that there were people who were wounded down there, people who were sick. And if possible, I asked him to have us moved up. I don't know whether he intervened. I don't know what the reason was, but they really did move me and two or three other men. I remember Ivan Keskic, who really was wounded in the arm. I remember Dr. Dzapic. And I don't know whether there was someone else. And they moved us into a room which was on one of the floors above. And then some sort of mission visited us. There were three persons dressed in white, and they were accompanied by Stjepan Vukadin, Dr. Zlatko Strujic, Dr. Hrvoje Lucic, Sister Pavka, and Bruno Batinic, a priest. They brought us some sandwiches and they asked us whether anyone was ill, if anyone needed medicine. These two doctors were there and asked us about this. Is there anything else you would like me to tell you about? These soldiers followed them immediately and they started --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I please stop you here for a while. This delegation you were just talking about, did they ask you questions? And if so, were you allowed to answer their questions?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was going to say. When these gentlemen arrived, they were followed by the soldiers and some sort of chiefs, and they almost prevented them from speaking to us. They would just say, "As you can see, everything is fine. There's nothing for you to do here. You can see the people. Everything's fine." We weren't able to say anything. We didn't have any time. They didn't let us speak. Assessed the situation. I was sitting at the back. I pulled the sleeve of this priest. He half turned. I put a piece of paper in his hand -- that was the list of people that I had on me -- and I pulled him by the sleeve, and again I pointed to the basement. I said, "Most of the people are down there." And then they more or less pushed them out of the room. The door was still open, and this priest said, "Well, are you going to show us the basement and the people who are in the basement?" And at that point they started shouting that there was no one else in the building, and so on. And someone from the International Community - I don't know who they were - someone said, "Take us down to the basement." The door then closed. And later on I found out that they insisted on being taken to the basement. They refused to leave before they took them to the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, you were just saying that when these gentlemen arrived, when you were making reference to the delegation you were talking about, they were followed by the "soldiers and some sort of chiefs and they almost prevented them from speaking to us." Can you please explain to us what you mean by saying "some sort of chiefs."

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, the person who received us from the basement, well, in my opinion he was some sort of a chief because he was issuing orders to others and said, "Take them away. Take out the items you have in your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pockets," and so on. Later when I asked, they told me he wasn't a man from Bugojno or from Donji Vakuf, because most of the soldiers there were soldiers from Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Mrso, whether you have been visited by a representative of the Muslim military other than Enes Handzic?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. When we went down to the basement, someone from Enes's service, Sabic, whom I know, about 15 of us entered the basement. He came into the basement and started hurling abuse at us. He almost started beating us and so on. He said, "What do you want, Ustashas? We're going to kill all of you." He cursed us, et cetera. I said, "What's wrong with you? Are you a man or an animal? Are you normal?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Someone from Enes's service, are you making reference to Enes Handzic?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Enes Handzic. Later I found out that he was some sort of a commander. That's where Enes Handzic was a chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mrso, did you know or did you get to know what the position of this Mr. Sabic has been at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I found out once I'd got out. I asked about this, since I know him. I know his father. I know everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are very close to the break. If you would allow me some additional three minutes, I could conclude this particular portion of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, do you recall a prisoner with the name Mario Zrno - Z-r-n-o - Mario Zrno being detained with you at the old convent building?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you recall whether this Mario Zrno was taken out for work details?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Three soldiers appeared and said, "We need five or six volunteers to do some sort of work." One, two, or three persons volunteered; the others didn't. They then designated them and took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you recall, Mr. Mrso, how Mario Zrno looked like when he came back from the work detail?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, how should I put this? He seemed scared, beaten, covered in blood, yellow, weak. He was barely able to stand. And naturally, we asked him what had happened. And then the others who were with him told us about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what had happened?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, they said that they'd been taken to the village of Vrpec or Crnice and that they had to bury some dead people. And the local people and soldiers who were there who were there attacked them. They were beaten with spades. They threw stones at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge, Mr. Mrso, whether the people who were taken out for work details were accompanied by Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: The soldiers took them out, and they said that they were the ones who took them there. Whether they were the same soldiers or some other soldiers, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would suggest to now have the break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Thank you. It's the time for the technical break. [Interpretation] We shall resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I give the floor to the Prosecution to continue with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, for how long have you been detained in the convent building?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Five days, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After these five days, were you released or were you transferred to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I was transferred to the basement of the secondary school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the details of the actual transfer, how did it happen.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I believe that it was on Friday, around 10.00 or between 10.00 and 11.00. A soldier came, asked me, Ivan Keskic and a third person to come out from the room on the first floor. They brought seven more people. They lined all of us up in the corridor. That's where we stood for some time. There were some soldiers there. An acquaintance of mine, that is, a neighbour of mine had a camera. He took our photos. And after a little while, three soldiers took us away. One was walking in front of us; two were walking behind us, or one was walking in the middle. They took us through the town. This was for the first time that I went through the town so I was looking around. As we were passing through the town, there were some people standing on the sidewalks who were shouting at us. I thought that we were being taken for execution, to be honest with you. And when we stopped walking, we were in the secondary school in the basement, in one of the cells in the basement of the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, you were telling us that all this happened on the Friday around 10.00. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the date, which day and which month was this Friday.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It was July. I can't give you the exact date, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was it more in the beginning of July, the middle of July, or more towards the end of July?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It was towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were walked from the convent building accompanied by soldiers, you were telling us that people were shouting at you. Did these people do anything else, other than shouting?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They also threw stones at us, and we had to protect our heads with our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the soldiers accompanying you, did they do anything in order to stop it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the soldiers accompanying you, were they the same soldiers that guarded you in the old convent building?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I suppose so. However, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were they Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber where you were brought to.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: We were brought to the basement of the grammar school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this grammar school also known as the Mahmut Busatlija building or Mahmut Busatlija school?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, that was its name, Mahmut Busatlija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What happened to you and the other detainees which were with you once you arrived at this school building?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They put us in the basement. There were other people in that cell. The cell was full. I didn't know how many of us were there at the time. Finally, when the cell was completely full, there were 42 of us there. They brought in some other people after I was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the size of the cell in which 42 people were detained.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I believe that it was 8 metres long, some 4 metres wide. It had a wire -- a wire door -- an iron door. I went to school there, so I knew this area from before. However, I had never measured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The 42 prisoners detained in the cell measured 4 metres by 8 metres, as you were saying, were they all soldiers or were civilians amongst them?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we were all civilians there. There were two women amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about the sanitary conditions in this cell with the 42 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know what you're referring to. There were no sanitary conditions. We didn't have a toilet. We did not have water. This was a very dirty room. The window was blocked with boards. It was lacking air. And we were lined up like sardines in a can. It was very hard to breathe in that room. So I really don't know what you're referring to as sanitary conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It was the end of July, Mr. Mrso. Was it hot in the cell?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It was very hot. It was unbearable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, I'm now going to show you another photograph. It will appear on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the necessary photocopies are available for distribution.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. This is grammar school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the school building you were detained?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please again sign and date the copy in front of you.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution intends to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit number will be P58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, I'm now going to show you a further photograph. Again, it will appear on the screen in front of you and you will be provided with a hard copy. The necessary copies are available for distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the information of Defence and the Trial Chamber, again, this photograph has been taken in the course of the investigation against the two accused in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: This is one part of this basement of this cell, as we called it. I recognise the niche in the wall and I recognise the basement window. The window at that time was blocked with wooden boards. However, this furniture wasn't there when I was there. The whole space was empty, bare of any furniture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the room you were detained together with 42 other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please again sign and date this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the guards in the school building. Were they civilians or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They were soldiers. They wore military uniforms, and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And on the military uniforms of the soldiers who guarded you, were there any insignia?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Believe me, I did not pay any attention to that, but I assume that they had the same insignia as the previous ones that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were they Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. I even knew some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were there any other cells in the basement of this school building you may be aware of?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. There were two other cells. We could hear parts of conversations and shouts coming from elsewhere. And when I asked the people who were in my cell who was in those cells, they said they didn't know. They only said that they assumed that they were Croatian police officers. They were just assumptions. When we were let to go to the toilet and have a bite to eat, I learned who these people were. It was only then that I actually found out that the other cells were full of people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The other two cells, were they of a similar size as the cell you were imprisoned with 42 other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: One was the same as ours. I don't know about the third one. I only assume that it was of the same size, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long did you have to stay in this cell in the school building?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: From Friday, that evening we didn't go out to the toilet, they didn't give us any food. On the following day, they did allow us to go to the toilet and they gave us some food. They gave us a soup; I don't know what kind of soup it was. And then I found out who the other people in the other cells were, because they brought all of us together to the place where they gave us food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Mrso, when you were transferred to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. On the 1st of August - it was Sunday, in the evening - they took us out. They lined us up, asked us what their names were and where we were from. And it was actually late in the night, around 11.00, around midnight. They put us in a lorry, took us away. We found ourselves in front of the school Vojin Paleksic [Realtime transcript read in error "in Aleksic"]. They put us in the sports hall of that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And whom are you referring to, Mr. Mrso, when you are saying "they put us in the sports hall of that school"?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: The soldiers. They were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were they Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the transcript, Mr. Mrso, is written "we found ourselves in front of the school in Aleksic." Can you please identify the school. What was the name of the school?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Vojin Paleksic. It was an elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where is or was this Vojin Paleksic Elementary School located? In which town?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It was in Bugojno, in Ivo Andric Street. Across the road from the school there is my brother's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were all of the prisoners from the Mahmut Busatlija school brought to the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School in Bugojno, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: To the sports hall of that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who brought you to the sports hall of that school?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Some soldiers. They wore military uniforms and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were they Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you arrived in the sports hall of the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School, what happened to you and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: As we entered the sports hall, we started chatting. The room was very big and there was a lot of air, and all of a sudden somebody shouted, "Shut up. I'm going to kill you." Then we heard a burst of fire. We all fell on the ground. And from then on we just stayed put. We didn't dare move or stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School in Bugojno, how many other detainees were imprisoned in the same sports hall?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: When I heard that burst of fire, I threw myself on the floor. I believe that the fresh air knocked me out and I fell asleep. When I came to, I could see more people being brought in. So on that day, on Monday, at the end of the day I counted heads. And there were 373, 374, or 375 people altogether. I made a note of the number in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You actually counted the number of detainees.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just informing us, Mr. Mrso, that other prisoners would be brought in. Did you get to know where the other prisoners came from?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. From the camps that were set up at the very beginning; that's the cultural and sports hall, the furniture shop, the grammar school, the convent. Some even came from some private prisons in various villages. That's what I heard from people that I spoke to. At the end of the day, on Monday there were altogether 375 or 374 people together. I can't remember exactly how many. I even started taking their names, but I ran out of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, the furniture shop you were just mentioning, can you please inform the Trial Chamber where this furniture shop is located.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In the centre. How shall I put it? I can't remember the name of the street. There was also the headquarters of the Institute for Urbanism. My brother worked at that institute as its general director. And below the institute was this furniture shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This furniture shop, was it located in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the cultural hall you were mentioning, was this detention facility also located in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, very close by. Yes, very close to that furniture store.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did you also get to know, Mr. Mrso, who actually brought the other detainees from the different detention facilities you just listed, who brought them to the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, they said that it was the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber, Mr. Mrso, about the sanitary conditions in the sports hall of the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School whilst you were detained with 370 detainees.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: The hall was big and airy. There was no water inside. There was no toilet. Every time we had to relieve ourselves, we had to ask to be let out to use the school's toilet facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the food conditions.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: On the first two days, we did not have anything to eat. On the second day, in the evening three soldiers came in. Two of them were carrying a big pot and some five or six loaves of bread. And it turned out that these loaves of bread were stale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was this amount of food sufficient for 370 detainees?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. It was not enough. I believe that the capacity of that pot was some 10 litres and there were five or six loaves of stale bread, so no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, I'm now going to show you a further photograph. Again, the photograph will appear on the screen in front of you and you will be provided with a hard copy, please. And the copies are available for distribution. Mr. Mrso, can you please tell us what you can see on the photograph in front of you.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: This is the school. However, it has been refurbished and renovated. At the time, it was damaged. Its name is now the First Elementary School. It used to be the Vojin Paleksic School at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the information of the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel, this photograph has also been taken in 2002 in the course of the investigation against the accused Hadzihasanovic and Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please sign and date this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you give us an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, I'm now going to show you another photograph. Again, it will appear on the screen in front of you and you will, again, be provided with a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the copies are available for distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, that's the hall that I and the others were in. It's been cleaned up a bit now though, and there are markings on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this - just for clarification, Mr. Mrso - is this the sports hall of the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School you were detained with 370 other detainees?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please again, Mr. Mrso, can you please sign and date it.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
