utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, whilst you and the other detainees were detained in this sports hall, did you become aware of any beatings?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you have seen and/or heard in respect to beatings.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, for example, they would appear and call out -- all I can remember, Niko Dzaja. They called him out and took him away. And then later on we all listened to him screaming. We heard them beating him. We heard terrible shots, bursts of fire. So we were afraid and waiting to see who the next person would be, waiting to see who they would call out again. Then there was someone called Anto Bakula. They beat him so severely, and then he was half alive when they returned him. We took charge of him. He was unable to speak. We thought he was dying. We were angry. I was the first one to bang on the door. I told them to open the door. I said that the person was dying, that they should provide him with medical treatment. They then raised a racket and closed the door. Then we banged on the door again and pleaded with them, and then they took him away, after which they returned him. I don't know where they took him. But as far as I know, this person is still alive today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso --

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: And there were some others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who were the others? So far you mentioned two individuals which were beaten.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I remember a waiter from Poric. I think his name was Milicevic. And I can't remember the names of the others. But they started beating one person in the hall and then they took him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the ones who took the detainees out for the beatings you were just describing, were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Soldiers. And they would always carry rifles when they entered. Two or three of them would enter, while the others would wait at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were they Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The 370 detainees in the sports hall of the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School, were they in the majority civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, I would say that it was about fifty/fifty; or perhaps there were more civilians, about 60 per cent were perhaps civilians. But this is a rough guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic background of the detainees in the sports hall of the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Amongst the detainees, were there also women or were they all men?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In the sports hall, there were only the two women who had been with me in the basement and in the grammar school, Andjelka Marijanovic and her daughter, Ivana.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you ever been told by anybody why you were detained?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: At no time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you ever been interviewed during your detention in the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. They started interviewing people on the second or third day. Some soldiers entered and asked us to hand our papers over and our valuables, if anyone had any. They asked us to hand over everything we had. I ignored this. I didn't pay much attention to it. And then people would go, and they said, "You go too. Don't cause problems," and so on. So one afternoon, when there was no longer such a huge crowd, I went too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What were the issues, if you do recall, Mr. Mrso, which have been addressed in the course of such interviews?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What are you referring to exactly? When and where?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just informing the Trial Chamber, Mr. Mrso, that they started interviewing people on the second or third day and that soldiers had entered prior to the interviews. And the question is, Mr. Mrso: What sort of questions were you asked during the interview, if any?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. When it was my turn, that wasn't in the hall; it was in one of the rooms in the school on one of the floors. I met a person I knew there, someone from Duvnjak -- Ismet Duvnjak and a neighbour of mine. And when I saw them there, the gentleman asked me, "What are you doing here?" And I was brazen and I said, "Well, I didn't come of my own accord," and so on, and so on. But he said, "Well, yes, but how did it happen?" And so then I said, "Well, don't pretend you're crazy. Your men must have brought me and you must know why I'm here." So we had this official exchange. I assume they asked me for my personal details and my address, and so on and so forth. I don't even know whether I signed anything, whether I signed for the details I'd provided them with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long, Mr. Mrso, have you been detained in the sports hall of the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Until the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what happened on the 5th of August. I assume it's the 5th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: After the interview, on the following day - that was in the afternoon - they called 10 or 11 of us and they said, "You'll be released but you have to report to the police every day at 12.00. You know where the police station is." And we said, "Yes, of course," since we were all local people and then at about 5.00 they released us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the ones who released you, were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: They were all soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once released on the 5th of August, 1993, what did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Mrso, when you informed any Muslim officials in Bugojno about the experiences you had made in the convent building, in the Gimnazija building, and in the Vojin Paleksic Elementary School?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, if you mean at that time, when I was released, it wasn't until the next day that I went into town, although they had warned me not to go. They said it was dangerous. But I decided to go regardless of what might happen. I simply wanted to see the town and to see what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you go, Mr. Mrso, go to somewhere or to someone to complain about the experience -- experiences you and the other Croats had to go through?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: On the following day, when I went out, I went to the Bugojno parish church. I met a lot of people there. It was chaos. People were crying. No one knew anything about anyone. Families had been separated. There were old people, sick people who had remained. People were being collected from the surroundings of Bugojno. Some people had started fleeing and were unable to do so. It was terrible. Soldiers from UNPROFOR were present at the time. People begged them to drive them away, take them out of Bugojno. It was all-out chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In August 1993, Mr. Mrso, did you have contact to Mr. Dzevad Mlaco?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. As I knew what the law was, I then decided -- as I'm a party member, I can engage in party-related activities. So three or four days later, I went to the municipality in Luka, and said that I wanted to see Mlaco. So that's the sort of action I took at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what did you talk to Mr. Dzevad Mlaco when you met him in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I suggested that I should make some sort of programme for action, a plan of action. We said I should come in two or three days' time. In the meantime, I found out who else was in Bugojno, and I assembled three or four other persons. And then as a team we said that we would come to see Mlaco with that plan, and that's how we established this contact. I told him where I had been immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you inform him about the detention facilities you were detained prior to you talking him?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Not prior to talking to him, but I told him personally about this. We knew each other, so I told him that this is what I wanted. I even asked for the HDZ office -- I looked for the HDZ office, which was also in the municipality. He agreed with me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were informing the Trial Chamber, Mr. Mrso, that you were released on the 5th of August, 1993. Were all of the 370 prisoners detained in the sports hall of the Vojin Paleksic School released the same day?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. Only the ten of us were released, or perhaps eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to the remaining 360 detainees?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. After the stadium was designated as a campsite, the stadium that belonged to the Iskra Football Club and they were all moved there later on and some were captured, civilians and other soldiers who were found. So towards the end of August there were 547 people in the Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When were the detainees from the Vojin Paleksic School transferred to the Iskra Stadium, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I think it was immediately after my release, mid-August, if I remember this correctly. I have made a note of the date, but I would need to remind myself of it. I would need to consult my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just mentioning, Mr. Mrso, that in the Iskra Stadium there were by end of August or towards the end of August there were 547 people detained. How did you get to know that there were 547 people detained in the Iskra Stadium by the end of August 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Through contact with Mr. Mlaco. But when I'd contact him, two Croats would always accompany me, two Croats from a group that we had formed. And as I knew what was happening, on the basis of reports from the camps and on the basis of some Muslim guards and soldiers, I asked for something to be done to improve the conditions. There should be a law, because there were minors there, an MP there, and according to the law he had to act and have them released. People should be allowed to receive food, because they had complained and said they had nothing to eat. I said that they shouldn't beat the soldiers. The soldiers should be able to receive mail, because the families were concerned about them and so on, et cetera. So in agreement with him, I went to see the camp commander and told him about what had to be done. He said, "I haven't been ordered to do anything." People would take food there of their own accord. Some people would be -- handed over this food. Others weren't allowed to receive it. So whenever I had contact with Dzevad Mlaco -- first it had to do with the conditions of the detainees in the camp and then about allowing a doctor or priest to have access to the camp. So these are the sort of agreements we tried to reach in the group of which I was a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These more than 500 detainees in this stadium, to your knowledge, were they civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, there were soldiers and civilian, but there were more civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You just mentioned there were minors amongst them.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long, to your knowledge, Mr. Mrso, have these 400 -- or more than 500 people, mostly civilians, been detained in the FC Iskra Stadium in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, through my contact with Mr. Mlaco, I also established contact with representatives of the International Community, representatives of the European Mission, and representatives of UNPROFOR. I would also submit reports to them and inform them of what was happening. And occasionally they released some people. The end of the camp was on the 19th of March, 1994. And at that time, there were 292 detainees in the camp, at the time the camp was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, I'm now going to show you a further photograph. It will again appear on the screen in front of you and you will be provided with a hard copy. And the copies are available for distribution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the information of the Chamber and Defence counsel, this photograph has also been taken in the year 2002 in the course of the investigation against the accused Hadzihasanovic and Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on the photograph in front of you.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: On the side of the street, I can see the stadium, the stalls -- the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this building which you can see on this photograph, is it the FC Iskra Stadium you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But here, the fence you can see here, the barbed wire is missing. It used to surround the entire stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber where to your knowledge in this building the about 540 prisoners were detained.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In these areas beneath the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Mrso, can you please date and sign the hard copy of the photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have an exhibit number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, the Iskra Stadium, was it guarded?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were the guards soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were they Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: During the time, Mr. Mrso, you took care of the detainees in the FC Iskra Stadium, did you ever talk to somebody, to a representative from the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. First with Dzevad Mlaco as the president of the War Presidency. He then told me that it wasn't his responsibility. He said it was Enes Handzic's responsibility. He referred me to Enes Handzic, so I went to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you recall, Mr. Mrso, roughly as to when you talked to Mr. Enes Handzic?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, the first time I attempted to speak to him, I can't remember the exact date but I think it was towards the end of August or, rather, at the beginning of September or perhaps in mid-September, when I was told that some Croatian soldiers who were in Prusac, in the direction of the Serbian lines, they were there as a human shield and they had to dig trenches there. I was told that they'd been moved to the Iskra Stadium. I went to look for Handzic, and he told me I should come the next day in the morning about 11.00. When I went there, the guard told me that he wasn't there. Niko Dzaja was then transferred, as well as Strujic and others. And I was told that these people were in the basement, in the cultural sports centre, which is where Enes Handzic had his office at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And this Mr. Enes Handzic you talked to at the beginning of September or perhaps in mid-September 1993, was it the very same Enes Handzic who had visited you in the old convent building in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what exactly did you inform Mr. Enes Handzic about?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I didn't find him at the time. I went to see Mlaco again. I told him I didn't find him, that he was avoiding me. That's what his guard told me, the same person who used to work in the company that I was the general manager of. He told me that discreetly. He didn't want it to be known that he had told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you found Mr. Handzic and had the opportunity to talk to him?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, when a detainee's wife came to see me. This person had been transferred from the stadium to the BH bank. When his family went to see him, they were not allowed to see him. They told them to wait until the moment his whereabouts were no longer known. His wife and daughter came to see me and told me, "Everybody who is transferred from the stadium is lost to their families." Then I went to see Mlaco, and I went to see Handzic. His office was transferred in the meantime. I told him that people had been detained and tortured in the camp below the bank. I told Handzic, "Sir, you're responsible. Why are these people disappearing?" I was too open when I put my questions to him. He told me, "I'm not responsible." I said, "Who is responsible?" And he says, "Tahir Granic." Very well, then. I know him. I know all of them. They're all natives of Bugojno. So he referred me to Tahir Granic, who was at that time the commander of the 307th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did you actually get an opportunity to talk to Tahir Granic, the commander of this 307th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He received me, although his aide-de-camp wouldn't allow me to talk to him. But I knew Tahir. I insisted on seeing him. I told him what was going on in the camp. I said I first talked to Mlaco, he referred me to Hadzic. Hadzic denied responsibility. "He told me, Tahir, that you are responsible. I want to know what's going on. I'm going to report you to international organisations." He says, "Don't do that. I don't know why they sent you to me. He is in charge. Go back and see him. I don't know why you've come to see me. I'm not in charge."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The 307th Brigade, Mr. Tahir Granic was the commander of, did it form part of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I suppose so. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the English transcript, but you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know whether this is a good time. However, the Prosecution knows very well the names of all the armies that were in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. And throughout the examination-in-chief of this witness, they're referring to the Muslim army. There is the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina with its proper name, so I would kindly ask the Prosecution to use the official names of the armies that they are questioning the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I give the floor to the Prosecution again. Please take into consideration the observation put forth by the Defence about the proper names of the military formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I certainly take note of the observations of the Defence; however it's the witness himself who uses the description "Muslim army," and the Prosecution doesn't want to put any words in the mouth of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right; the witness has indeed spoken about the Muslim army. However, when you are putting questions to the witness, maybe you can ask him whether he is aware of the proper name of this Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, you heard the comments made by both Defence counsel and the Presiding Judge. Are you aware of the proper name of the Muslim army you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In our local conditions, this is the name that we used. We knew that those were Muslims and we referred to it as the Muslim army. At that time, I didn't know the proper name of that army. When Muslims attacked Croats in Bugojno, some month or a month and a half after I left the camp they said, "When we attacked you, when we occupied you," and all of a sudden they started talking about a conflict. At first it was an attack, and then it was a conflict. These were our discussions at the local level. I really don't know when the BH army received this name, when it was named the BH army. And that's why I'm referring to the army as the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, we were about -- you were about to inform the Trial Chamber about your meeting with Mr. Tahir Granic, the commander of the 307th Brigade of the army you are referring to as the Muslim army. When did this meeting with Mr. Tahir Granic take place?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I believe that it was in December. I can't recall the exact date. I believe that it was towards the end of December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you recall, Mr. Mrso, where this meeting with Mr. Granic took place?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In the building of the Koprivnica forestry company. This is where their headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please provide -- can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the details of this conversation with Mr. Tahir Granic.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I asked him what was going on in the camp. I mentioned the terrible conditions there. I mentioned that people kept on going missing from the camp, and I also told him that my fellow Croats kept on insisting about finding out the whereabouts of these people who went missing from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Which camp, Mr. Mrso, are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: The Iskra Stadium camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Granic's response to your complaint?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Mr. Granic told me, literally: "Mrso, I have nothing whatsoever to do with this. Handzic is in charge of that. He is the only person who can provide you with answers." I told him that "people are being sent to Uskoplje and Gornji Vakuf, to the positions where they are in peril of being injured and this has to come to an end." He replied, "I understand all that. However, I am not responsible. It is Enes Handzic who is in charge and who is responsible for all that."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were mentioning earlier on, Mr. Mrso, that you informed representatives of the International Community, of organisations of the International Community which were active during this time period in the area of Bugojno about the events you were describing today.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber which international organisations these people were members of.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It was the International Red Cross; then UNPROFOR; the European Mission. And I believe that these were the people who were in Bugojno at the time that I reported to about what was going on. I informed them about the treatment of Croats. I implored with them to have the conditions in the camp improved. However, they were not allowed to enter the camp, so we complained to each other. The people who were in charge of the camp were constantly in discord with representatives of the international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you recall, Mr. Mrso, even if it's roughly only, as to when for the first time or as to when you started to inform members of UNPROFOR, the Red Cross, and the European Monitoring Mission about the situation in the camp?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: As soon as the camp was established as the central camp. I went there immediately after that. On one occasion, I even spoke with some of the detainees over the fence. I often went to see Sadikovic, who was in charge of the camp. I asked him to allow families to bring food to the detainees. I often spoke with UNPROFOR representatives, representatives of the European Mission who also came to me. It was my duty to inform them and to ask their assistance, and I would really very often talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At the time you informed the members of the international organisations you were just referring to, was the camp - and I understand you are referring to the FC Iskra Stadium - was it still used as a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: If you're expecting my answer, sir, I really don't understand what the question was. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was it already 1993, Mr. Mrso, when you informed the representatives of ECMM and/or UNPROFOR and/or the Red Cross about the fact that the FC Iskra Stadium was used as a detention camp?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you recall the month when you for the first time informed them about the FC Iskra Stadium?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: In late August, then in early September. And from then on, throughout the existence of the camp I constantly informed them about the conditions in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Late August, early September means late August of 1993 and early September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, do you still recall any names of the representatives of the international organisations you were talking to in 1993 about the conditions in the FC Iskra Stadium in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: These were not conversations. These were my complaints and my implorations for help. I remember a Dutch man, Rudi. There was a Spanish guy, Garcia Jesus. There was a person from Greece. There were some French men. However, I cannot recall any of their names. I would have to consult my notes; then I'd be able to tell you. There was Mr. Banks from UNPROFOR. There was an Englishman. I apologise. I don't have my diary, so I don't want to speculate on people's names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Dutch person called Rudi -- was it Rudi Gerritsen? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I cannot recall this gentleman's family name, not without my notes, not without my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These individuals you were just detailed, were they members of ECMM and/or UNPROFOR or both?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I believe that they were from the European Community. This Mr. Rudi, Jesus Garcia, this person from Greece whose name I can't recall, they were all representatives of the European Community. And also the French men whose names I can't remember, they were also representatives of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what was the reaction, if any, by the representatives of the International Community you talked to about the situation in the FC Iskra Stadium?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: To be honest, this all boiled down to their promises that they would talk with the representatives of the other side, that this was not part of their mandate. I didn't know that at the time. I was not very satisfied with their answers, but I simply had to take what I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, at the beginning of your today's testimony, you were informing the Trial Chamber that by end of 1993 only 900 Croats out of the about 16.100 Croats living in Bugojno prior to the war were still in Bugojno. Do you think or do you know whether the events you were testifying today about were the reason that the Croats, that about 15.000 Croats left Bugojno in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, those were the reasons. People were attacked, robbed. Money was asked from them. People were ill-treated. They didn't feel safe, and they just fled. They paid Muslims to take them out. Dautovic himself organised help for them to leave. They collected money from people who then came and complained to me. They were never taken out. So they even organised a public protest in front of the police administration building asking for money back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mrso.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the Prosecution's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It is 25 to 6.00. We are going to make a break, a technical break. And we shall resume at 6.00 and we will end today's session at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Defence counsel starts its cross-examination, there's just one matter I would like to clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said at the very beginning of your testimony that when you saw the Muslims arriving from abroad you saw some of them with headbands and others had sort of armbands. And you said that in your opinion they were MOS members. On their armbands were -- was the inscription "MOS" contained on it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not what I said for those foreigners. That's what I said about the Muslim soldiers. I said that the foreigners wore strange clothes. They had turbans or some sort of head scarfs. They had short trousers. I could recognise them on the basis of their colour. But I didn't say that they had these bands, nor that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you said that the MOS -- what you said about the MOS concerned the local soldiers.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: That's correct. Because there was graffiti on the wall, and you can see this graffiti to this very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "MOS," what does that mean in your language?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know. I asked Muslims whom I knew, and they said the "Muslim Liberation Forces." And I didn't ask them anything else and I wasn't interested in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it's an Arab word then.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It's the abbreviation for "Muslim Liberation Forces." Those are the letters with which these words begin, "MOS."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for having clarified this. We have one hour left. Defence counsel may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Mrso. My name is Edina Residovic, and I represent General Hadzihasanovic. I would like to put some questions to you, but first of all, since you were involved in agriculture for a long time and you then got involved in politics, Mr. President, I would first of all like to ask this witness some questions of a general nature, as I think that the witness could answer them. And they would be of interest for the defence of General Hadzihasanovic. Mr. Mrso, you said that you were born in Bugojno and that at the beginning of the war you also lived in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you didn't spend your entire working life in Bugojno. You spent a significant part of your life and you also worked as a prominent agriculturist in Modrica, in Northern Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that in 1968 you got married to a Muslim woman, Mubera Hadzijusufovic is her name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had two daughters with her; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber that you got divorced in 1978, but that you got officially divorced in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. My information was not correct.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I apologise, but you can check with the Bugojno court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's not at all necessary. I just wanted to check your personal details, because you've already been a Defence witness and we just want to check your credibility was a witness. Mr. Mrso, as in the proceedings themselves my colleagues and my colleagues from the Prosecution, and the Trial Chamber too, most likely -- as it will help all of us to understand the overall situation if we inform them of the events in Bugojno and its surroundings, I would first of all like to show you part of a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that we could pinpoint the exact geographic location of Bugojno. And you have testified about Bugojno today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher show this part of the map to the witness in order for us to identify certain places in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, if you've had a look at the map, could you put it on the ELMO, which is next to you, and use a pencil to mark the places that I will mention, places which I believe you know. This is in order to be able to ask you some questions about these places. First of all, could you mark the place called Bugojno with number "1."

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it with number "1."

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can encircle the number to make it more visible.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say - and this is for the sake of the transcript - that we have now marked Bugojno with number "1"? This is where you lived during the war. Could you now mark Zenica with number "2."

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript: The witness has marked Zenica with number "2." Mr. Mrso, would it be correct to say that up until the war Bugojno was part of the Zenica district in situations when districts were referred to? For example, when people spoke about the district court or the high court, it belonged to that regional community. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, in administrative terms, that is how people referred to this. They would say "the district court" and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now mark Travnik with number "3."

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, Novi Travnik has now been marked with number "3."

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, you said Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said Travnik, but you have marked Novi Travnik, which is a little to the north. I think Travnik is a little further to the north. Could you mark Travnik with number "4." It's just below Vlasic. That's where it is. Can you see? Mark it with number "4."

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, Novi Travnik has been marked with number "3" and Travnik has been marked with number "4." Could you please mark Donji Vakuf with number "5." And you have testified about Donji Vakuf today.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: With number "5"?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, the witness has marked Donji Vakuf with number "5." Could you mark Gornji Vakuf with number "6".

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, Gornji Vakuf has been marked with number "6". And could you now mark Prozor with number "7".

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, Prozor has been marked with number "7". Mr. Mrso, please keep the map in front of you, as some questions will concern the geographical position of Bugojno. Mr. Mrso, is it correct to say that Bugojno is in the upper part of the Vrbas estuary in Central Bosnia in the so-called Skopaljska Valley? That is correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That valley is between the mountain Vranjica and Radusa. It's about 30 kilometres long and 6 to 8 kilometres wide, depending on the position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you go upstream the River Vrbas, there is the town of Gornji Vakuf, which you have been marked with number 6 on this map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But I think it's 18 kilometres from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that better than I do. I don't know the geography of the place, so I do accept that it might be 18 kilometres upstream, 18 kilometres away. Downstream at --

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- 12 kilometres is the place called Donji Vakuf, which you have marked with number 5; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, is it correct to say that Bugojno is connected to Travnik by an asphalt road which passes through Donji Vakuf and the Komar mountain pass and then it continues through the Lasva Valley, which connects it with Zenica and Sarajevo? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. And there is another route for Travnik which goes through Ravno Rostovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you. At the beginning of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina the Serbian forces occupied Donji Vakuf and the Komar mountain pass, the combat lines were very near the town. They were only a few kilometres from the town. So the route about which I asked you a minute ago, through Komar, could not be used to go to Travnik or Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say that for certain, because I didn't use that route. On one occasion, I set off, when there was an incident. At the time, I was in Sarajevo and couldn't get out of Travnik. That was on the 28th of February, 1992 or 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to ask you about now. Since there could have been problems there - you're not sure about that - the inhabitants of Bugojno used this alternative route, which was partially a dirt road and partially an asphalt road, and it went through the Rostovo plateau towards Novi Travnik and Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, Bugojno is also connected to the southern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and especially to Herzegovina, by a road which goes through Gornji Vakuf and Prozor towards Jablanica and Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a road which led to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: It went through the Neretva Valley in the direction of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But because of the wartime operations and because bridges had been destroyed, that road was no longer practicable. A country road, a road through the mountain in the direction of Mostar was used. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These routes through Gornji Vakuf and Prozor were under HVO control in 1992 and 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since I have asked you all the questions that relate to this map, I suggest this map be admitted into evidence. And could the witness write the date on the map and sign it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I sign this? Since I have said that I don't know who controlled those roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've just marked geographical positions on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your answer has been recorded but -- has been noted, but as we need to have a record of the questions that are put, with regard to the roads I would like to ask you to write your name down on this document, sign the document, and make a note of today's date. Today it's the 9th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll show this document to the Prosecution and to the Defence, to the accused. And Mr. Registrar will give us an exhibit number. This is a document for Mr. Hadzihasanovic's defence. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be DH25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH25. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, you said that towards the end of 1990 -- or, rather, at the beginning of 1991 you joined the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, it was a year and a half before the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: If that is what you think. At the moment, I don't know exactly when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your party, the HDZ, got the greatest amount of votes in the elections in 1990 in the municipality of Bugojno, but it didn't have an absolute majority and was thus not able to assume power; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I know that it had the most votes, it won the most votes, but I'm not certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, by cooperating with other parties, Vladimir Soljic, the HDZ president, was elected as the major of Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Soon after the elections, you noticed that the SDS - the Serbian political party, the Serbian Democratic Party - started arming the Serbian population of the municipality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know about that, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, because of the events in Croatia - we're talking about 1991 - and because of the war in Croatia, the HDZ started arming the Croatian population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know about that, because I didn't participate in such things -- if the HDZ was engaged in those activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although Bosnia and Herzegovina had legally elected representatives in the elections, HDZ representatives on the 18th of November 1991 took the decision to form the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I don't know about that. When you said that I was involved in agriculture and politics, I wouldn't agree with that because I was never a politician. These -- such were the situations in Bugojno, and because of the situation I got involved in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I could agree with you, but the situations can turn a man into a politician. And you were practically a politician from --

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: From 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From 1993 up until today.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Up until today? No, that's not correct. I apologise for this clarification. I I'm not involved in any party activities, you know, and because of the laws and so on, conflicts of interest. I work in the parish. I work in the county.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity of reading the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you were aware of the fact that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had been established.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, through the radio, and if I had the opportunity of reading the newspapers, given the situation, because we were cut off. I have to inform you of the fact that we were unable to communicate with anyone from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, through the radio and the newspapers and as a member of your party, you were probably aware of the fact that within -- that there were 30 municipalities in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and Bugojno was one of them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Believe me, to this very day I know nothing about this, because that aspect was not something I was interested in. I didn't participate directly in those matters. I lived in Bugojno and I wasn't present at meetings or agreements with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you know not only that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established but also the Croatian Defence Council, which was the military organ of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, through the media. But as for the details, the dates, I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are also aware of the fact that the Croatian Defence Council as a political and military leadership structure was formed in the area of Bugojno too.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the HVO was the president of the HDZ, Mr. Vladimir Soljic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know anything about that. I don't want to burden the Trial Chamber with this, because there were disagreements among us, the party and later on the Crisis Staff that was then established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you were a member of the town committee of the party, you're telling us that you don't know who the president of the highest organ of the Croatian people in Bugojno was; is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: For the sake of the truth, you should be aware of the fact that those military structures had forbidden party activity in Bugojno -- HDZ activity, that is to say. But I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that in May 1992 the HVO headquarters issued an order establishing that throughout the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna the only legitimate military units were HVO units and all orders and all the military units of the Territorial Defence were proclaimed to be illegal? Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. And, Mr. President, I would be grateful if such questions weren't put to me, because I did not participate in such policies, either as a party member or a citizen of Bugojno. This was not part of my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, Defence counsel has to represent the accused. That is their duty. And in the course of their cross-examination, which is taking place at the moment, they may ask you questions to see whether you are a credible witness, to establish what the reality that you have described was. And they may also place you within a political context, as you said at the beginning when answering the Prosecution's questions. You said you were an HDZ member. As a result, the Defence is asking you to provide them with certain clarifications. Now, if you don't know the answers, just tell us. If you don't know the people in question, inform us of this fact. The Defence has the right to ask you questions, and you should just say, "I know the answer," or, "I don't know the answer"; "I don't know these people." It's up to you to say what you want to say, but you should answer the questions nevertheless. Be aware of the fact that this isn't a burden for the Trial Chamber, because the Trial Chamber is here to obtain a general idea of what happened and in particular in terms of the policies pursued. Mrs. Residovic, please continue with your questions. But if the witness says that he doesn't know an answer, then he doesn't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, although this witness has not confirmed that he is aware of the documents that I've referred to, I'm still going to present these documents to the witness. And I would kindly ask the Chamber to take them into account because the Defence is going to tender these documents into evidence at a later stage. I'm talking about the Official Gazette and the decision on the establishment of Herceg-Bosna and the order pursuant to which the legitimate Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina are proclaimed illegal. I would like these two documents to be shown to the witness and to be given to my learned friends and all those present in the court. I would like these documents to be identified as documents that the Defence has presented to the witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, before I give the floor to the Prosecution, you're talking about documents in B/C/S and translations into English.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just explain. These are a few documents that the Defence has come across in the course of the investigation of other cases; in this particular case, these are documents that were obtained by the Prosecution in the Martinovic/Naletilic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution will object to any attempt to tender documents into evidence to which the witness is not able to comment on. Only documents in regard of which the witness is in a position to make a statement, only such documents can be tendered into evidence. Otherwise, there is no relation between the witness's evidence and the documents Defence wishes to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We have noted what you have just said. We are going to retire for a couple of minutes to deliberate on this issue. Please stay in the courtroom. We will be back shortly. --- Break taken at 6.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Before we render our decision on these documents, we're going to show the documents to the witness and we shall wait for his answer. So I'm going to ask the usher to give these two documents to the witness. We also need to avail ourselves of the documents in order to examine their contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I please address the Honourable Chamber? Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my information, it is the practice of this Tribunal that some documents which are relevant are accepted. Some are just identified, with the obligation on the part of the Defence to tender these documents into evidence at a later stage. If this is not done, then documents do not become exhibits. We have opted for the stricter option, because we believe that these documents are relevant and also because of the fact that this Trial Chamber has already adopted such practice. A document which was shown to the Witness XP [as interpreted], and the witness did not recognise it, did not have anything to say about the document, the Prosecution did tender this document into evidence and the Chamber has admitted it just as being identified. So we believe that we followed a practice that has already been adopted by this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, the two documents - as far as I understand, you have two documents - have been provided to you by the Prosecution; is that correct? I am turning towards the Defence. These two documents, you have been provided with these documents from the Prosecution or are they something that you have come across during your own investigation? What is the origin of these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence asked to gain access to other documents which were conducted before this Tribunal; Naletilic, Kordic, Kupreskic cases. The documents that I am showing to you today have been taken from the Naletilic/Martinovic case as tendered by the Prosecution and admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that the documents that you are showing to us are documents that you have obtained and that they were tendered by the Prosecution in other cases. So this is the origin of the documents. Before we decide on the admittance of these documents, I would like to give the floor to Mr. Withopf for some additional explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution is questioning the relevance of the contents of these documents for the current proceedings. Defence counsel may please, if they wish to do so, explain the relevance of the fact, if so, that the only legal military unit in the territory of the HZ HB are the units of the HVO in respect to the current proceedings. The Prosecution can't see any relevance of both of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The only problem that we have to solve is that the Prosecution asks from the Defence to tell the truth what is the relevance of these documents with respect to the case that we are dealing with here. What can you tell us about the relevance of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in keeping with Rule 89(C), the Trial Chamber may admit into evidence any document that has some probative value. We have not tendered these documents; although, we believe that they have quite a substantial probative value for the defence of our corps commander because they speak about the establishment of a para-state community in the area where the 3rd Corps was operating. The town of Bugojno is in that community. In the entire area, the only armed force which could exist in keeping with the 1992 constitution was the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So these are the reasons which, at a later stage, ended up in a conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as the Defence is going to show at a later stage. So from the point of view of everything that happened in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, these documents are indeed relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We have noted your position regarding the relevance of these documents. Let's move on and show these documents to the witness who is going to tell us whether he is familiar with them or not. And then we shall render our decision. Madam Usher, can you please show these two documents to the witness. The witness already has these two documents. Defence, you can ask your questions which arise from these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, again I'm asking you whether you saw this decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which was published in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Again, under oath: This is the first time I see this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, did you know that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn at a later stage that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established and were you the person who communicated with the most responsible persons of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No, I couldn't do that, because I could not leave Bugojno and I didn't know who these persons were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of October 1993, together with the European monitor who was a Greek national, did you travel to the centre of Herceg-Bosna and did you meet with the president of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Defence Council, Mr. Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, you were aware of the position of Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: No. I went to him as the president of my party. At that moment, I didn't know what other positions and duties were -- did he have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, regardless of this answer, because of the relevance of these documents, we propose that these documents be identified and we shall tender these documents into evidence at the moment when we have witnesses who will be able to tell us something about these documents from their personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you have the floor. Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution opposes against such a procedure. Number one, the witness has answered all questions in relation to this document with "no"; and, number two, the document is not of any relevance for the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We are going to retire for a brief deliberation. We shall be coming back shortly. --- Break taken at 6.48 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. We're going to communicate our oral decision on the motion of the Defence to admit the documents that the Defence obtained from another case. Both cases are Prosecution exhibits. After having deliberated on this issue, we would like to establish that these documents -- as regards their relevance, as far as the witness is concerned, the witness is not aware of these documents so these documents cannot be tendered through this witness. This witness has just told us that, A, he was not aware of the existence of this document; and, B, as far as the author of this document is concerned - and that is Mr. Mate Boban - he said that he had met Mr. Mate Boban, but he doesn't know what his official position was at the time. At this moment, the documents cannot be admitted into evidence. You will have an opportunity to ask for their admittance at a later stage at the moment when you have a witness who's aware of their existence or if the Defence tenders a series of documents into admission, please do that. But as far as this witness is concerned, this witness is not aware of these documents and we cannot admit them. We believe that the moment is not right for these documents to be admitted. In any case, keep them and move for their admittance at a more convenient moment for the Defence. You may proceed with the cross-examination of this witness. We have another ten minutes or so, but we will of course continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, you said that Mr. Vladimir Soljic was the president of the HVO and the HDZ in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: The HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: The HVO? I'm not aware of that. The HDZ. It was Matko Lucic at the time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Vladimir Soljic was the mayor of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know Mr. Soljic?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will kindly ask the witness to be shown a photo and I will ask the witness to recognise Vladimir Soljic on that photo, if he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. There is a Vladimir Soljic from Bugojno and there is also a Vladimir Soljic from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show this person from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't see him in this photo. I can't see a Vladimir Soljic from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know other persons who are depicted in this photo?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this photo is so unclear that it is very hard for me to recognise anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then ask the witness to return the photo. The Defence is not going to tender this photo into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Defence does not insist. Maybe, Mr. Withopf, your intervention is not necessary. The witness has not recognised anybody, and the Defence is not tendering this into evidence. What were you going to say, Mr. Withopf?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very briefly, just for future cases. The Prosecution draws the attention of the Trial Chamber that on this photograph there actually are names mentioned. If the Defence asks a witness to identify a person on a photograph, the names shouldn't be detailed on the very same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is just a technical matter. So you are not insisting on this photo being tendered into evidence. Witness, can you please return the photo to Madam Usher, who is going to return all the photos to the Defence. And we're also returning all the other documents that haven't been tendered into evidence at this stage. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrso, are you aware of the fact that the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was before the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed this decision anti-constitutional?

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: To be honest, I did not follow this. This is not within my scope of activities in the party or in my professional life. I never paid attention to any such thing. I never registered any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do we continue until 7.00 or quarter past 7.00? Just one last question for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally it is 7.00. You have one last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the municipal committee of the HDZ of Bugojno, in spring 1993 you participated at a meeting in Travnik at which the political and military situation in the territory of Central Bosnia was discussed.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, it was on the 8th of April, 1993, that you attended the meeting of all the representatives of the HDZ and HVO in Travnik, during which you discussed a political and military situation.

utterances.speaker: IVO MRSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will be all for today, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as you know, the Defence has not finished its job. They still have questions to ask you. Unfortunately, you will have to return tomorrow afternoon, when we resume. So I am going to ask you to come back to the same place. In the meantime, you are not going to meet with anybody. You're not going to meet either with the representatives of the Prosecution or the representatives of the Defence. You are here to testify to the truth, and the only persons you're supposed to talk to are the members of the Chamber. So we kindly ask you to come back tomorrow, and hopefully we'll be able to finish your cross-examination tomorrow. Thank you very much for coming. Madam Usher is going to take you out of the courtroom, and we kindly ask you to come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are free to go, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, can we go -- please go for just one minute into private session. I have to make an announcement in respect to the witness schedule for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall move into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
